claim: Tuberculosis (TB) has been the first cause of death by an infectious disease for years surpassing HIV according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
source: Tuberculosis (TB) has been the first cause of death by an infectious disease for years surpassing HIV according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to WHO as an authoritative source on global disease burden.

claim: In 2019 there were 10 million new TB cases and 1.4 million deaths.
source: In 2019 were reported 10 million new TB cases and 1.4 million deaths, with these numbers likely to increase due to the COVID-19 pandemic (Glaziou, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Glaziou, 2020.

claim: TB case numbers are likely to increase due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: In 2019 were reported 10 million new TB cases and 1.4 million deaths, with these numbers likely to increase due to the COVID-19 pandemic (Glaziou, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Glaziou, 2020.

claim: Recent transmission significantly contributes to the global TB-burden mostly in high incidence regions.
source: Recent transmission significantly contributes to the global TB-burden mostly in the high incidence regions and its control is imperative to achieve the goal of the End TB Strategy (Auld et al., 2018; Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015; Yates et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Auld et al., 2018; Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015; Yates et al., 2016).

claim: In low-burden countries, TB cases are mainly contributed by re-activations of latent TB infection (LTBI) from recently arrived migrants.
source: On the contrary, in low-burden countries the assumption is that transmission plays a minor role, supported by the fact that in countries close to the pre-elimination phase (<5/100,000 cases) TB cases are mainly contributed by re-activations of latent TB infection (LTBI) from recently arrived migrants (Menzies et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Menzies et al., 2018.

claim: Whole genome sequencing (WGS) displays higher resolution and provides accurate results tracking recent transmission.
source: The WGS displays higher resolution, provides accurate results tracking recent transmission (Jajou et al., 2018; Marais et al., 2017; Meehan et al., 2019; Nikolayevskyy et al., 2019), and reports greater agreement with epidemiological results than previous molecular markers (Diel et al., 2019; Meumann et al., 2021; Nikolayevskyy et al., 2016; Roetzer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Jajou et al., 2018; Marais et al., 2017; Meehan et al., 2019; Nikolayevskyy et al., 2019).

claim: WGS reports greater agreement with epidemiological results than previous molecular markers.
source: The WGS displays higher resolution, provides accurate results tracking recent transmission (Jajou et al., 2018; Marais et al., 2017; Meehan et al., 2019; Nikolayevskyy et al., 2019), and reports greater agreement with epidemiological results than previous molecular markers (Diel et al., 2019; Meumann et al., 2021; Nikolayevskyy et al., 2016; Roetzer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Diel et al., 2019; Meumann et al., 2021; Nikolayevskyy et al., 2016; Roetzer et al., 2013).

claim: A cut-off of 5 SNPs has been widely accepted for the clustering of recently linked cases.
source: A cut-off of 5 SNPs has been widely accepted for the clustering of recently linked cases (Meehan et al., 2019; Nikolayevskyy et al., 2019) while an upper value of 12 SNPs also incorporates older transmission events (Walker et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Meehan et al., 2019 and Nikolayevskyy et al., 2019.

claim: An upper value of 12 SNPs incorporates older transmission events.
source: A cut-off of 5 SNPs has been widely accepted for the clustering of recently linked cases (Meehan et al., 2019; Nikolayevskyy et al., 2019) while an upper value of 12 SNPs also incorporates older transmission events (Walker et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2013.

claim: The study sequenced the whole genome of 785 Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains from Valencia region.
source: We sequenced the whole genome of 785 Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains and linked genomes to patient epidemiological data.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's methodology and sample size.

claim: About 1388 TB cases were reported between 2014 and 2016 by the Valencian Regional Public Health Agency (DGSP), with 1019 having positive culture.
source: About 1388 TB cases were reported between 2014 and 2016 by the Valencian Regional Public Health Agency (DGSP), 1019 with positive culture.
evidence: This is a direct statement of epidemiological data from the study.

claim: 785 samples were collected from 18 regional hospitals.
source: All the available (785) samples were collected from 18 regional hospitals (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's sample collection.

claim: Demographic, clinical, and microbiological records were obtained for 724 of the total samples.
source: Demographic, clinical, and microbiological records were obtained from the routine TB surveillance system, for 724 of the total samples.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data available for analysis.

claim: The study sequenced 77% of the TB culture-positive cases reported between 2014 and 2016 in Valencia region.
source: We sequenced 77% of the TB culture-positive cases reported between 2014 and 2016 in Valencia region with a 4.3 million population.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's coverage of culture-positive cases.

claim: Six different lineages (L) were identified circulating in the Valencia region.
source: We identified 6 different lineages (L) circulating in the region (Coll et al., 2014; Stucki et al., 2016), with L4 the most frequent (92.1%) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: L4 was the most frequent lineage in Valencia region at 92.1%.
source: We identified 6 different lineages (L) circulating in the region (Coll et al., 2014; Stucki et al., 2016), with L4 the most frequent (92.1%) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TB incidence in Valencia region ranged between 8.3 and 8.7 cases per 100,000 inhabitants.
source: TB incidence in the region ranged between 8.3 and 8.7 with higher incidence in migrants (mean 23.6) than in local born individuals (mean 6.9).
evidence: This is a direct statement of epidemiological data from the study.

claim: TB incidence was higher in migrants (mean 23.6) than in local born individuals (mean 6.9) in Valencia region.
source: TB incidence in the region ranged between 8.3 and 8.7 with higher incidence in migrants (mean 23.6) than in local born individuals (mean 6.9).
evidence: This is a direct statement of epidemiological data from the study.

claim: 63% of all TB cases in Valencia region were Spanish-born patients.
source: remarkably 63% of all cases were Spanish-born patients, while 30% came from high-incidence countries, and 7% from other low-incidence countries.
evidence: This is a direct statement of epidemiological data from the study.

claim: 30% of TB cases in Valencia region came from high-incidence countries.
source: remarkably 63% of all cases were Spanish-born patients, while 30% came from high-incidence countries, and 7% from other low-incidence countries.
evidence: This is a direct statement of epidemiological data from the study.

claim: 7% of TB cases in Valencia region came from other low-incidence countries.
source: remarkably 63% of all cases were Spanish-born patients, while 30% came from high-incidence countries, and 7% from other low-incidence countries.
evidence: This is a direct statement of epidemiological data from the study.

claim: Diabetes was present in 10.4% of TB cases in Valencia region.
source: When we observed risk factors associated with TB, we found that diabetes was present in 10.4% of cases; although this was more prevalent in Spanish-born patients (OR 2.7, CI 1.5–5.4, p<0.001), values were similar to diabetes prevalence in the general Spanish population.
evidence: This is a direct statement of epidemiological data from the study.

claim: Diabetes was more prevalent in Spanish-born TB patients (OR 2.7, CI 1.5–5.4, p<0.001).
source: When we observed risk factors associated with TB, we found that diabetes was present in 10.4% of cases; although this was more prevalent in Spanish-born patients (OR 2.7, CI 1.5–5.4, p<0.001), values were similar to diabetes prevalence in the general Spanish population.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis from the study.

claim: Conventional contact tracing investigations identified 66 epidemiological clusters, including 97 cases, accounting for 12.5% of transmission in the Valencia region.
source: Conventional contact tracing investigations (see Methods) identified 66 epidemiological clusters, including 97 cases, accounting for 12.5% of transmission in the Valencia region (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of epidemiological data from the study, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Using a 12 SNP threshold, 112 genomic clusters were identified, including 331 (42.7%) patients.
source: Considering the widely used pairwise distance threshold of 12 SNPs for defining transmission, we identified 112 gClusters, including 331 (42.7%) patients, with cluster size ranging from 2 to 12 cases (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of genomic clustering results from the study, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Cluster size in Valencia region ranged from 2 to 12 cases using a 12 SNP threshold.
source: Considering the widely used pairwise distance threshold of 12 SNPs for defining transmission, we identified 112 gClusters, including 331 (42.7%) patients, with cluster size ranging from 2 to 12 cases (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of genomic clustering results from the study, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Spanish-born patients were more likely to be part of genomically linked groups (OR 2, CI 1.44–2.79, p<0.001).
source: Although these clusters included foreign-born patients, Spanish-born patients were more likely part of genomically linked groups (OR 2, CI 1.44–2.79, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis from the study.

claim: 42 genomic clusters exclusively comprised Spanish-born patients.
source: In this regard, 42 gClusters exclusively comprised Spanish-born patients and 8 included only foreign-born patients.
evidence: This is a direct statement of genomic clustering results from the study.

claim: 8 genomic clusters included only foreign-born patients.
source: In this regard, 42 gClusters exclusively comprised Spanish-born patients and 8 included only foreign-born patients.
evidence: This is a direct statement of genomic clustering results from the study.

claim: Pulmonary localization of TB was associated with clustering (OR 2.5, CI 1.60–3.98, p<0.001).
source: In addition to Spanish origin, pulmonary localization of TB (OR 2.5, CI 1.60–3.98, p<0.001), and younger age also appeared associated with clustering by Fisher's exact test.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis from the study.

claim: Younger age was associated with clustering.
source: In addition to Spanish origin, pulmonary localization of TB (OR 2.5, CI 1.60–3.98, p<0.001), and younger age also appeared associated with clustering by Fisher's exact test.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis from the study.

claim: After correcting for confounders using logistic regression, Spanish origin remains significantly associated with clustering (p<0.001).
source: After correcting for confounders using a logistic regression, Spanish origin remains significantly associated with clustering (p<0.001); younger age, pulmonary localization of TB, and male sex were also significant (p<0.05, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis from the study.

claim: Younger age, pulmonary localization of TB, and male sex were significantly associated with clustering after correcting for confounders (p<0.05).
source: After correcting for confounders using a logistic regression, Spanish origin remains significantly associated with clustering (p<0.001); younger age, pulmonary localization of TB, and male sex were also significant (p<0.05, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis from the study.

claim: 90% of TB cases in Valencia region are susceptible to all antibiotics used in treatment.
source: Finally, 90% of TB cases in Valencia region are susceptible to all antibiotics used in treatment, so resistance has no impact on clustering.
evidence: This is a direct statement of drug susceptibility data from the study.

claim: Resistance has no impact on clustering in Valencia region.
source: Finally, 90% of TB cases in Valencia region are susceptible to all antibiotics used in treatment, so resistance has no impact on clustering.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high proportion of drug-susceptible cases.

claim: Independently of the SNP cut-off considered, the clustering rate obtained by contact tracing was always lower than the genomic estimates.
source: We also assessed gClusters considering lower SNP thresholds, and observed that independently of the cut-off considered, the clustering rate obtained by contact tracing was always lower than the genomic estimates (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of comparison between contact tracing and genomic clustering, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: A high number of genomic links were not detected by epidemiological investigation.
source: A high number of genomic links were not detected by epidemiological investigation, while some epidemiological links were not corroborated by any gClustering threshold (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of comparison between epidemiological and genomic data, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Some epidemiological links were not corroborated by any genomic clustering threshold.
source: A high number of genomic links were not detected by epidemiological investigation, while some epidemiological links were not corroborated by any gClustering threshold (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of comparison between epidemiological and genomic data, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Only 15.4% of the 331 patients within genomic clusters (12 SNPs) had an identified epidemiological link.
source: Comparison of both approaches revealed that only 15.4% of the 331 patients within gClusters (12 SNPs) had an identified epidemiological link (Appendix 1, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of comparison between epidemiological and genomic data.

claim: A ROC curve establishes 11.5 SNPs as the optimal value for the SNP cut-off that maximizes the agreement between epidemiological investigation and genomic data, with an area under the curve higher than 0.9.
source: A ROC curve establishes 11.5 SNPs as the optimal value for the SNP cut-off that maximizes the agreement between epidemiological investigation and genomic data, with an area under the curve higher than 0.9 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis from the study, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Oxfordshire displayed a bimodal pattern for clustering, with transmission groups clearly differentiated from unlinked cases with distances higher than 50 SNPs.
source: We observed a bimodal pattern for Oxfordshire, with the transmission groups clearly differentiated from the other unlinked cases with distances higher than 50 SNPs.
evidence: This is a direct statement of clustering pattern analysis from the study.

claim: For Valencia region and Malawi, strains group in a large range of distance thresholds (SNPs 0–150), showing continuous clustering throughout the distance values.
source: For the Valencia region and Malawi, strains group in a large range of distance thresholds (SNPs 0–150). Thus, there exists a continuous clustering throughout the distance values.
evidence: This is a direct statement of clustering pattern analysis from the study.

claim: A strict transmission threshold of 12 SNPs does not apply to all settings when analyzing transmission dynamics, particularly in places with higher transmission burdens.
source: The results strongly suggest that a strict transmission threshold of 12 SNPs (or any other threshold) does not apply to all the settings when analyzing transmission dynamics, particularly in those places with higher transmission burdens (Figure 3A), and specially if we want to understand long-term transmission (i.e. the survival and expansion of particular clones/strains in a population).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of clustering patterns across different settings.

claim: The oldest genomic cluster in Valencia region dated to around 30 years before the sampling period.
source: The Valencia region's oldest gClusters dated to around 30 years before the sampling period.
evidence: This is a direct statement of dating analysis from the study.

claim: When considering only strains epidemiologically linked, the oldest most recent common ancestor can be traced less than 10 years.
source: When considering only strains epidemiologically linked, the oldest most recent common ancestor can be traced less than 10 years.
evidence: This is a direct statement of dating analysis from the study.

claim: A 12 SNP threshold identifies both recent and older transmission events.
source: Thus, a 12 SNP threshold identifies both recent and older transmission events.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dating analysis of genomic clusters.

claim: A 5 SNP threshold dates clusters between 1999 and 2015 in agreement with recent transmission.
source: A 5 SNP threshold dates clusters between 1999 and 2015 in agreement with recent transmission rendering more actionable results for public health, as was previously shown (Jajou et al., 2018; Meehan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement of dating analysis from the study, supported by citations.

claim: In Oxfordshire, 14 transmission links were identified between 5 and 25 years before 2016, with the next transmission link being inferred between 100 and 150 years before 2016.
source: In the case of Oxfordshire, we identified 14 links between 5 and 25 yB 2016, with the next TL being inferred between 100 and 150 yB 2016 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement of transmission link analysis from the study, with reference to figures.

claim: A gap of 75 years occurs between the most recent and the oldest transmission links in Oxfordshire.
source: Thus, a gap of 75 years occurs between the most recent and the oldest TLs, explaining why the 12 SNP threshold performs well in this setting as a transmission marker.
evidence: This is a direct statement of transmission link analysis from the study.

claim: In Malawi, 70 transmission links dated back to 50 years before 2016 and 46 dated between 50 and 150 years before 2016.
source: In the case of Malawi, we counted 70 links dating back to 50 yB 2016 and 46 dated between 50 and 150 yB 2016 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—source data 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of transmission link analysis from the study, with reference to figures.

claim: For Valencia region, 143 transmission links dated back 50 years before 2016 and 43 between 50 and 150 years before 2016.
source: For the Valencia region, we counted 143 links that dated back 50 yB 2016 and 43 between 50 and 150 yB 2016 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplements 3–6, Figure 3—source data 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement of transmission link analysis from the study, with reference to figures.

claim: The gap detected in Oxfordshire is not observed in Malawi or Valencia.
source: The gap detected in Oxfordshire is not observed in Malawi or Valencia.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing transmission link patterns across settings.

claim: There was no difference when comparing the age of the patients belonging to a genomic cluster with the inferred age of the cluster (Welch two-samples t-test, p-values>0.1).
source: We found no difference when comparing the age of the patients belonging to a gCluster with the inferred age of the cluster (Welch two-samples t-test, p-values>0.1, Appendix 1—figure 3, Supplementary file 7), suggesting that the strains included in this study do not represent reactivations and that uninterrupted transmission is the most likely explanation for the old links observed.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis from the study.

claim: The strains included in this study do not represent reactivations and uninterrupted transmission is the most likely explanation for the old links observed.
source: We found no difference when comparing the age of the patients belonging to a gCluster with the inferred age of the cluster (Welch two-samples t-test, p-values>0.1, Appendix 1—figure 3, Supplementary file 7), suggesting that the strains included in this study do not represent reactivations and that uninterrupted transmission is the most likely explanation for the old links observed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of patient age and cluster age.

claim: The percentage of genomically linked cases (12 SNPs) in Valencia region was around 43% in the total population.
source: The percentage of genomically linked cases (12 SNPs) of around 43% in the total population, increases to 47% among the Spanish-borns being 31% among imported cases, suggesting that transmission among locally born patients majorly contributes to disease burden.
evidence: This is a direct statement of genomic clustering results from the study.

claim: The percentage of genomically linked cases (12 SNPs) increases to 47% among Spanish-born patients in Valencia region.
source: The percentage of genomically linked cases (12 SNPs) of around 43% in the total population, increases to 47% among the Spanish-borns being 31% among imported cases, suggesting that transmission among locally born patients majorly contributes to disease burden.
evidence: This is a direct statement of genomic clustering results from the study.

claim: The percentage of genomically linked cases (12 SNPs) was 31% among imported cases in Valencia region.
source: The percentage of genomically linked cases (12 SNPs) of around 43% in the total population, increases to 47% among the Spanish-borns being 31% among imported cases, suggesting that transmission among locally born patients majorly contributes to disease burden.
evidence: This is a direct statement of genomic clustering results from the study.

claim: Transmission among locally born patients majorly contributes to disease burden in Valencia region.
source: The percentage of genomically linked cases (12 SNPs) of around 43% in the total population, increases to 47% among the Spanish-borns being 31% among imported cases, suggesting that transmission among locally born patients majorly contributes to disease burden.
evidence: This is an inference based on the higher clustering rate among Spanish-born patients.

claim: Clustering rates in Valencia region remain high when considering a stricter threshold of 5 SNPs (35 vs. 39% for total vs. Spanish-born).
source: These percentages remain high when considering a stricter threshold of 5 SNPs for clustering (35 vs. 39%, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct statement of genomic clustering results from the study.

claim: Higher transmission was found in Valencia region compared to other population based studies conducted in low-burden settings, where clustering rates ranged between 14 and 16%.
source: We found higher transmission in the Valencia region compared to other population based studies conducted in low-burden settings, where clustering rates ranged between 14 and 16% (Jajou et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2014) and somewhat closer to that reported in mid and high TB-incidence settings (39–85%) (Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015; Gygli et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2019; Saavedra et al., 2022; Walker et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022; Yates et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison with other studies, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Clustering rates in mid and high TB-incidence settings ranged between 39–85%.
source: We found higher transmission in the Valencia region compared to other population based studies conducted in low-burden settings, where clustering rates ranged between 14 and 16% (Jajou et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2014) and somewhat closer to that reported in mid and high TB-incidence settings (39–85%) (Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015; Gygli et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2019; Saavedra et al., 2022; Walker et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022; Yates et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison with other studies, supported by multiple citations.

claim: High transmission among Spanish-born individuals is a major contributor to disease burden in Valencia.
source: High transmission among Spanish-born individuals is a major contributor to disease burden in Valencia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering analysis.

claim: Reactivation of infections in imported cases from high-burden settings is the significant driver in other low-burden settings.
source: By contrast, reactivation of infections in imported cases from high-burden settings is the significant driver in other low-burden settings (Jajou et al., 2018; Kamper-Jørgensen et al., 2012; Meumann et al., 2021; Walker et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with other studies, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The results reveal the heterogeneity of the TB epidemic among settings, highlighting the lack of correlation between a region's TB burden and the level of local transmission.
source: Thus, our results reveal the heterogeneity of the TB epidemic among settings, highlighting the lack of correlation between a region's TB burden and the level of local transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of transmission dynamics across different settings.

claim: In low-burden TB settings, comparison between contact tracing and WGS revealed that between 38 and 57% of genomically linked cases had also an epidemiological link.
source: In low-burden TB settings, comparison between contact tracing and WGS revealed that between 38 and 57% of genomically linked cases had also an epidemiological link (Diel et al., 2019; Jajou et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with other studies, supported by multiple citations.

claim: In high-burden settings, the agreement between contact tracing and WGS is significantly lower (8–19%).
source: In high-burden settings, which suffer from rampant community transmission (Yates et al., 2016), the agreement between both approaches is significantly lower (8–19%) (Auld et al., 2018; Middelkoop et al., 2015; Verver et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a comparison with other studies, supported by multiple citations.

claim: In Valencia region, the agreement between contact tracing and WGS was similar to high-burden settings (15.4%).
source: In the Valencia region, we observed an agreement similar to high-burden settings (15.4%), meaning that almost 80% of transmission is missing by the health system, despite contact tracing being conducted in 78% of cases.
evidence: This is a direct statement of comparison between contact tracing and genomic data.

claim: Almost 80% of transmission is missing by the health system in Valencia region, despite contact tracing being conducted in 78% of cases.
source: In the Valencia region, we observed an agreement similar to high-burden settings (15.4%), meaning that almost 80% of transmission is missing by the health system, despite contact tracing being conducted in 78% of cases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low agreement between contact tracing and genomic data.

claim: Contact tracing among household close contacts will not have a significant effect on TB incidence at a community level in settings like Valencia region.
source: As has suggested for high-burden settings, contact tracing among household close contacts will not have a significant effect on TB incidence at a community level (McCreesh and White, 2018; Surie et al., 2017), since much of transmission may result from casual contact in community settings between individuals not known to one another (Auld et al., 2018; Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015) and also, transmission associates more with social drivers, including the ways in which individuals interact and congregate (Andrews et al., 2014; Mathema et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the low agreement between contact tracing and genomic data, supported by citations.

claim: Much of transmission may result from casual contact in community settings between individuals not known to one another.
source: As has suggested for high-burden settings, contact tracing among household close contacts will not have a significant effect on TB incidence at a community level (McCreesh and White, 2018; Surie et al., 2017), since much of transmission may result from casual contact in community settings between individuals not known to one another (Auld et al., 2018; Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015) and also, transmission associates more with social drivers, including the ways in which individuals interact and congregate (Andrews et al., 2014; Mathema et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: Transmission associates more with social drivers, including the ways in which individuals interact and congregate.
source: As has suggested for high-burden settings, contact tracing among household close contacts will not have a significant effect on TB incidence at a community level (McCreesh and White, 2018; Surie et al., 2017), since much of transmission may result from casual contact in community settings between individuals not known to one another (Auld et al., 2018; Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015) and also, transmission associates more with social drivers, including the ways in which individuals interact and congregate (Andrews et al., 2014; Mathema et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: Community transmission is behind the lack of agreement between genomic and epidemiological clusters observed in Valencia region.
source: Thus, our results support that community transmission is behind the lack of agreement between genomic and epidemiological clusters observed in the Valencia region, and highlights its relevance in low burden settings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison with high-burden settings and the low agreement between contact tracing and genomic data.

claim: Community transmission is relevant in low burden settings.
source: Thus, our results support that community transmission is behind the lack of agreement between genomic and epidemiological clusters observed in the Valencia region, and highlights its relevance in low burden settings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings in Valencia region.

claim: Most epidemiologically linked cases have a common ancestor less than 10 years before the most recent sample.
source: Most of the epidemiologically linked cases have a common ancestor less than 10 years before the most recent sample, and the distance between samples typically ranged between 0 and 4 SNPs, with only one individual link separated by 11 SNPs (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of dating analysis from the study.

claim: The distance between epidemiologically linked samples typically ranged between 0 and 4 SNPs, with only one individual link separated by 11 SNPs.
source: Most of the epidemiologically linked cases have a common ancestor less than 10 years before the most recent sample, and the distance between samples typically ranged between 0 and 4 SNPs, with only one individual link separated by 11 SNPs (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of genomic distance analysis from the study.

claim: Strains linked by more than 5 SNP are beyond the action of public health interventions as they involve too old transmission links.
source: While the ROC curve indicated a 12 SNP threshold to capture most epidemiological links, the reality is that strains linked by more than 5 SNP are beyond the action of public health interventions as they involve too old TLs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dating analysis of genomic clusters and epidemiological links.

claim: Events useful for public health investigations are better captured by a 5 SNP threshold even though some epidemiological links are missing.
source: Our results imply that events useful for public health investigations are better captured by a 5 SNP threshold even though some epidemiological links are missing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dating analysis and comparison with epidemiological data.

claim: Even when using a 5 SNP threshold, public health only identifies around 15% of the cases in genomic clusters.
source: But the reverse is also true, and more dramatic. Even when using a 5 SNP threshold public health only identifies around 15% of the cases in gClusters.
evidence: This is a direct statement of comparison between public health identification and genomic clustering.

claim: The many genomic links missed by public health investigations in Valencia region is similar to what is seen in high-burden countries, where contagion occurs outside the traditional household or work settings.
source: The many genomic links missed by public health investigations in Valencia region reminds of what is seen in high-burden countries, where contagion occurs outside the traditional household or work settings.
evidence: This is a comparison with high-burden settings based on the low agreement between contact tracing and genomic data.

claim: Valencia region and Malawi display continuous and sustained transmission links over time.
source: Furthermore, the Valencia region and Malawi also display continuous and sustained TLs over time (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a direct statement of transmission link analysis, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Events outside the genomic transmission clusters likely reflect older contagion chains that still contribute to TB incidence today.
source: Those events outside the genomic transmission clusters likely reflect older contagion chains that still contribute to TB incidence today, as a consequence, clustering is continuous in settings exhibiting this transmission dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the continuous clustering pattern observed.

claim: Clustering is continuous in settings exhibiting sustained transmission dynamics.
source: Those events outside the genomic transmission clusters likely reflect older contagion chains that still contribute to TB incidence today, as a consequence, clustering is continuous in settings exhibiting this transmission dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the continuous clustering pattern observed.

claim: The lack of effective past efforts to halt transmission may represent a plausible explanation for continuous transmission in Valencia region.
source: The lack of effective past efforts to halt transmission may represent a plausible explanation.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of continuous transmission.

claim: Spain suffered from higher disease incidence for most of the 20th century, reflecting its lower socioeconomic status than neighboring countries.
source: The higher transmission and the older age of transmission chains likely reflects a situation in which Spain suffered from higher disease incidence for most of the 20th century, reflecting its lower socioeconomic status than neighboring countries.
evidence: This is an inference based on historical context and the observed transmission patterns.

claim: Improved TB control has led to a continuous drop in case numbers and to an incidence from 22 to 6.4 in the last 20 years in Valencia region.
source: Improved TB control has led to a continuous drop in case numbers and to an incidence from 22 to 6.4 in the last 20 years.
evidence: This is a statement about epidemiological trends in Valencia region.

claim: Oxfordshire displays a bimodal distribution of clustering across pairwise distances.
source: By contrast, Oxfordshire displays a bimodal distribution of clustering across pairwise distances, and also lacked transmission events other than those involving 12 SNP gClusters (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement of clustering pattern analysis, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Oxfordshire lacked transmission events other than those involving 12 SNP genomic clusters.
source: By contrast, Oxfordshire displays a bimodal distribution of clustering across pairwise distances, and also lacked transmission events other than those involving 12 SNP gClusters (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement of transmission link analysis, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The robust reduction in both disease incidence and transmission occurred until the beginning of the 1990s in the UK.
source: These results agree with the robust reduction in both disease incidence and transmission that occurred until the beginning of the 1990s in the UK; after that, increased HIV infections, immigration and the emergence of TB drug resistance fueled the expansion of TB (Glaziou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Glaziou et al., 2018.

claim: After the 1990s, increased HIV infections, immigration and the emergence of TB drug resistance fueled the expansion of TB in the UK.
source: These results agree with the robust reduction in both disease incidence and transmission that occurred until the beginning of the 1990s in the UK; after that, increased HIV infections, immigration and the emergence of TB drug resistance fueled the expansion of TB (Glaziou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Glaziou et al., 2018.

claim: Ongoing transmission in Oxfordshire was dated back to 1993.
source: In accordance with this data, we dated ongoing transmission in Oxfordshire back to 1993.
evidence: This is a direct statement of dating analysis from the study.

claim: The results imply uninterrupted transmission of TB in Valencia region and Malawi and not in Oxfordshire.
source: Our results imply uninterrupted transmission of TB in Valencia region and Malawi and not in Oxfordshire and offer an explanation for the differences in SNP distributions across settings (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the transmission link analysis across different settings.

claim: The results offer an explanation for the differences in SNP distributions across settings.
source: Our results imply uninterrupted transmission of TB in Valencia region and Malawi and not in Oxfordshire and offer an explanation for the differences in SNP distributions across settings (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the transmission link analysis across different settings.

claim: The results underscore a primary role for continuous transmission in fueling TB incidence in Valencia region.
source: Our results underscore a primary role for continuous transmission in fueling TB incidence in the Valencia region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transmission link analysis.

claim: Community transmission is occurring more frequently in Valencia region rather than in household contacts.
source: Likewise, our results strongly suggest that in this particular setting, community transmission is occurring more frequently rather than in household contacts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low agreement between contact tracing and genomic data.

claim: In other low-burden countries, transmission is limited and immigration from high-burden countries, also involving reactivation of the disease, represents the primary driver of incidence.
source: The opposite scenario occurs in other low-burden countries (Jajou et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2014) where transmission is limited and immigration from high-burden countries, also involving reactivation of the disease, represents the primary driver of incidence (Meumann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison with other studies, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Meta-analysis from historical epidemiological studies suggests that, contrary to current assumptions, MTB infection may not be lifelong, and most people are able to clear it.
source: In addition, reported meta-analysis from historical epidemiological studies suggests that, contrary to current assumptions, MTB infection may not be lifelong, and most people are able to clear it (Behr et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Behr et al., 2019.

claim: The prevalence of LTBI is much lower than assumed, and most of the TB cases we see today are coming either from recent contagion or imported depending on the TB setting.
source: This further suggests that the prevalence of LTBI is much lower than assumed, and most of the TB cases we see today are coming either from recent contagion or imported depending on the TB setting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the meta-analysis findings cited.

claim: Low burden does not translate to low transmission.
source: We demonstrate that low burden does not translate to low transmission, highlighting how low-burden TB locations can entail very distinct scenarios that require specifically tailored management in order to eliminate TB, and that general guidelines should not be applied to all the areas based solely on incidence rate (Lönnroth et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of transmission dynamics across different settings.

claim: Low-burden TB locations can entail very distinct scenarios that require specifically tailored management in order to eliminate TB.
source: We demonstrate that low burden does not translate to low transmission, highlighting how low-burden TB locations can entail very distinct scenarios that require specifically tailored management in order to eliminate TB, and that general guidelines should not be applied to all the areas based solely on incidence rate (Lönnroth et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of transmission dynamics across different settings, supported by citation.

claim: General guidelines should not be applied to all areas based solely on incidence rate.
source: We demonstrate that low burden does not translate to low transmission, highlighting how low-burden TB locations can entail very distinct scenarios that require specifically tailored management in order to eliminate TB, and that general guidelines should not be applied to all the areas based solely on incidence rate (Lönnroth et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of transmission dynamics across different settings, supported by citation.

claim: In areas where incidence is mainly contributed by transmission, actions beyond passive case finding strategies are likely to be more successful.
source: In areas where incidence is mainly contributed by transmission, actions beyond passive case finding strategies are likely to be more successful.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings about transmission dynamics.

claim: Different forms of active case finding to cut community transmission have been implemented in low income countries that can be transferred to high and middle income ones.
source: Different forms of active case finding to cut community transmission have been implemented in low income countries that can be transferred to high and middle income ones (Ho et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ho et al., 2016.

claim: There is the opportunity to move toward genomics-informed infection control programmes, e.g., by identifying transmission hotspots or highlighting unanticipated risk factors.
source: Those strategies can be designed not only based on the presence of social and host risk factors (Dowdy et al., 2012) now there is the opportunity to move toward genomics-informed infection control programmes, e.g., by identifying transmission hotspots or highlighting unanticipated risk factors.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of genomic epidemiology.

claim: Active case finding has the potential to tackle subclinical TB transmission.
source: Active case finding also has the potential to tackle subclinical TB transmission, which we estimated using high resolution transmission mapping in our setting (Xu et al., 2019), and its impact on global and local TB control is still unknown (Kendall et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation about the potential of active case finding, supported by citations.

claim: The impact of subclinical TB transmission on global and local TB control is still unknown.
source: Active case finding also has the potential to tackle subclinical TB transmission, which we estimated using high resolution transmission mapping in our setting (Xu et al., 2019), and its impact on global and local TB control is still unknown (Kendall et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kendall et al., 2021.

claim: Understanding heterogeneities in TB transmission dynamics is essential to define tailor-made interventions to halt transmission with a population-level impact.
source: Our key message is that understanding heterogeneities in TB transmission dynamics is essential to define tailor-made interventions to halt transmission with a population-level impact, which is key to reducing the incidence of TB worldwide.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Halting transmission with a population-level impact is key to reducing the incidence of TB worldwide.
source: Our key message is that understanding heterogeneities in TB transmission dynamics is essential to define tailor-made interventions to halt transmission with a population-level impact, which is key to reducing the incidence of TB worldwide.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Clustering in Valencia region is higher (47.4%) than in Oxfordshire (27%), and similar to a high-burden area as Malawi (49.8%).
source: Our results underscore significant differences in transmission between low-burden TB settings, i.e., clustering in Valencia region is higher (47.4%) than in Oxfordshire (27%), and similar to a high-burden area as Malawi (49.8%).
evidence: This is a direct statement of comparison of clustering rates across settings.

claim: Settings with high transmission rate are associated with decades of uninterrupted transmission, irrespective of burden.
source: By modeling times of the transmission links, we observed that settings with high transmission rate are associated with decades of uninterrupted transmission, irrespective of burden.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transmission link analysis across different settings.

claim: Burden and transmission are not necessarily linked due to the role of past epidemics in the ongoing TB incidence.
source: Together, our results reveal that burden and transmission are not necessarily linked due to the role of past epidemics in the ongoing TB incidence, and highlight the need for in-depth characterization of transmission dynamics and specifically tailored TB control strategies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of transmission dynamics across different settings.

claim: There is a need for in-depth characterization of transmission dynamics and specifically tailored TB control strategies.
source: Together, our results reveal that burden and transmission are not necessarily linked due to the role of past epidemics in the ongoing TB incidence, and highlight the need for in-depth characterization of transmission dynamics and specifically tailored TB control strategies.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Oxfordshire had an incidence of 8.4 cases per 100,000 inhabitants.
source: Here we use available datasets from a low burden setting (Oxfordshire, incidence 8.4 cases per 100,000 inhabitants) and from a high burden setting (Malawi, incidence 87 cases per 100,000 inhabitants) and compare to a newly generated dataset in Valencia region (incidence ~8 cases per 100,000 inhabitants).
evidence: This is a direct statement of epidemiological data for Oxfordshire.

claim: Malawi had an incidence of 87 cases per 100,000 inhabitants.
source: Here we use available datasets from a low burden setting (Oxfordshire, incidence 8.4 cases per 100,000 inhabitants) and from a high burden setting (Malawi, incidence 87 cases per 100,000 inhabitants) and compare to a newly generated dataset in Valencia region (incidence ~8 cases per 100,000 inhabitants).
evidence: This is a direct statement of epidemiological data for Malawi.

claim: Valencia region had an incidence of approximately 8 cases per 100,000 inhabitants.
source: Here we use available datasets from a low burden setting (Oxfordshire, incidence 8.4 cases per 100,000 inhabitants) and from a high burden setting (Malawi, incidence 87 cases per 100,000 inhabitants) and compare to a newly generated dataset in Valencia region (incidence ~8 cases per 100,000 inhabitants).
evidence: This is a direct statement of epidemiological data for Valencia region.

claim: In Oxfordshire, 92% of culture-positive cases were sequenced.
source: Sequences from two population-based studies in Oxfordshire (Walker et al., 2014), with 92% of culture-positive cases sequenced, and Malawi (Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015), with 72% of culture-positive cases sequenced, were downloaded from ENA and analyzed as for the sequences generated in this study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the coverage of sequencing in Oxfordshire.

claim: In Malawi, 72% of culture-positive cases were sequenced.
source: Sequences from two population-based studies in Oxfordshire (Walker et al., 2014), with 92% of culture-positive cases sequenced, and Malawi (Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015), with 72% of culture-positive cases sequenced, were downloaded from ENA and analyzed as for the sequences generated in this study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the coverage of sequencing in Malawi.
